title: My current take on AI and game/software development
author: MouradBakhali
selftext:
I could be completely wrong, but I don't think AI simply means “less work.”

When production gets cheaper, expectations tend to rise. We've seen this before with game engines.

 is going to push that pattern much further,and I think it will change not just how we make things, but what becomes expected from us as creators.

AI

I wrote down my thoughts on where this could lead.

[https://blog.qinteract.com/posts/cheap-production-more-expectations-more-work/](https://blog.qinteract.com/posts/cheap-production-more-expectations-more-work/)

I'd genuinely like to hear what you think, especially if you disagree with the argument.

comments.author: vlad_h
comments.body:
I agree with much of the mechanics here: cheaper production raises expectations, the baseline moves, and AI will keep reaching into parts of the work we currently think require human judgment.  
Where I diverge is in how I look at that.  
Once the argument becomes “AI can do this now, and eventually it may do this too, so what will be left for me?” we’ve moved from observing what is happening into worrying about what might happen. And I don’t find that particularly useful.  
Maybe AI eventually does most of what I do today. Fine. When that happens, I’ll figure out what to do with the capabilities available then. So far, I haven’t encountered many problems in life that became easier because I worried about them before they existed.  
What interests me much more is the opportunity. Every new thing AI becomes capable of doing gives me something else I can use. If it takes over another layer of my work, I don’t need to defend that layer. I can move somewhere else, build something different, or use the new capability to attempt something that wasn’t practical before.  
Maybe the job I have today disappears. Maybe the entire definition of the job changes. I don’t know, and neither does anyone else.  
When that problem actually exists, I’ll solve it. And if there’s nothing there worth solving, I’ll pivot.  
I’m much more interested in what becomes possible than in protecting what used to be necessary.

replies.author: MouradBakhali
replies.body: Yeah, I totally agree with you. We are not sure where this is heading, and there is no need to worry about a future problem that doesn't exist yet. If AI takes over a layer of work, that's another step we can level up to build things that weren't possible before.

comments.author: Alextuxedo
comments.body:
I mean, the fundamental thing about creative works is that they're mainly matters of taste, and very little is really objective about them. I think it's hard to say that everyone's expectations are just going to keep rising when plenty of older games with "worse" graphics are often still regarded as some of the best games that have ever been made.

Think about stuff like Super Metroid, the original MGS, and whatever other "classic" games you really enjoy. The technical limitations of those graphics technologies give them such distinctive quirks that people are actively trying to replicate those specific brands of "shittiness." Take the whole PS1 style craze that's going on right now.

And not to mention the fact that plenty of people are kind of disillusioned with the idea of completely massive games. Not saying that that's necessarily a *bad* thing, but there's certainly a case to be made for smaller projects. I don't have time to take on a 100 hr RPG at this time in my life, but an experience I can knock out in 5, or a run-based thing where a single go-around only takes about a half an hour? That's more accessible.

I also really don't mean to be rude to anyone here but the person / people behind the project matter and no matter how good AI gets it won't really change that. Do you have any level of understanding of art and animation? How about music? Storytelling? Programming and general software design? Any of the other countless disciplines that go into making a great game? 

Those fundamentally still matter and your knowledge of those subjects will help you refine your tastes, and the output of whatever tool you use. There are reasons most significant game projects made have taken massive teams and most solo projects take several years, sometimes even into the double digits.

Even if customers expectations rise, your knowledge and experience with those skills will help you to deliver on those higher expectations.

replies.author: MouradBakhali
replies.body:
I agree with most of what you say.

And to add to that. While writing this article I was wondering what we have to read, learn, and what kind of knowledge we need to acquire to refine our taste. The reason is I believe good taste will matter a lot when AI reach a point where it can make and judge anything.

replies.author: Alextuxedo
replies.body:
> While writing this article I was wondering what we have to read, learn, and what kind of knowledge we need to acquire to refine our taste

The answer is becoming competent in those disciplines more directly, and reading about and studying their histories. 

You are not going to be able to properly critique an AI's visual output if you do not understand and have no experience with drawing, painting, digital art, 3D modeling or some other medium where you start from nothing and build something up.

You will not be as effective at telling your AI agent to create music or sounds without understanding what goes into that process yourself, how to communicate what you want and how to refine or add to things by hand if nessesary. 

Again, I really don't mean to be a jerk in this regard, but there is value in understanding these deep skills. You will not be able to create something more original if you do not understand these things.

And it's not like you need to be Claude Monet or Beethoven to make decent art or music by hand. There are so many free online resources and open-source creative tools that you can use to start learning stuff by hand.

I'm so passionate about the field of gamedev because it has pushed me to engage with these skills in a deeper way, and I kind of feel like AI can degrade that in many ways.

Do you *need* to do everything by hand? Not anymore, but that doesn't mean that approach isn't valuable. 

Not to mention the fact that if you're making games as a solo dev for reasons other than personal enjoyment, I'd argue you're making the wrong decision. Not in every case, but especially if you believe you're going to make money doing it. 

Hundreds of games are being uploaded to Steam every day, and that's not considering all the other platforms and things that exist to share games. 

If you believe you're going to make a significant profit on a game, even one made entirely by hand with all the technical skill in the world, well, I don't wanna be an asshole and say "give up," but... the numbers are not in your favor. AI will not make those numbers any better.

Those are my reservations when it comes to a lot of this tech in general. As I said, I really don't wanna be a jerk; but in most cases you're probably not going to make a ton of money on game projects anyway, so I feel that the real value, for me at least, comes with learning all of the different things that go into making a game. AI won't necessarily push you in that same way, and I think it's that kind of push you really need to get better as someone who wants to make a good game.

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body: Exaclty. This is literally the entire story of humanity and tools. More advanced tools lead to more advanced creations not working less hard. In fact there’s anthropological evidence that the average hunter gatherer worked fewer hours than modern humans. We just keep shifting the role of the human vs the role of the tools.

replies.author: MouradBakhali
replies.body: I agree, it is the same pattern, again and again.
